what: The redness of the two-sitting stand that `pnpm run gate` admits, by name, with a ceiling and a date.

WHO ADMITTED IT, AND WHO HAS NOT. The orchestrator of step Ш6 did, on 2026-08-25, on its own authority and nobody else's. The owner has not seen this file, was not asked about it, and has agreed to none of it. That is what `ratifiedBy: null` on every line below means, and it means nothing weaker: not `unknown`, not `not applicable`, but the record that the three points still below are standing on one agent's decision, unreviewed. `tools/gate.mjs` prints it whenever the FULL gate reaches this budget at all, green or red, so that a green gate cannot be read as more than it is -- `gate:fast` never gets here, and neither does a run whose stand died before it judged. `tests/stand/allowance.ts` refuses a line that names the owner in `allowedBy` while `ratifiedBy` is null, because that is the exact sentence this file was first written with: all five lines it then carried said "owner, through the Ш6 orchestrator, 2026-08-25", and no owner had been asked. When the owner ratifies -- or refuses -- their name and the date go in `ratifiedBy`, and the line stops being one agent's word.

WHAT `null` DOES NOT MEAN. It does not mean the owner said no. There is no value of `ratifiedBy` for that, and there deliberately is not one: a line the owner has REFUSED is not an unreviewed permission, it is an overridden one, and it has no business standing in a budget. If the owner says no, the line is DELETED and the gate goes red -- that is the whole procedure. A union type distinguishing 'refused' from 'not asked' was considered and refused in turn: it would branch every place that reads the field and double the cases about it, for a state that has occurred nought times. So `null` is unambiguous, and it says one thing: nobody has been asked.

WHAT A RATIFICATION HAS TO CARRY. Not a name. A name alone was the quieter half of the same forgery: the gate says `allowedBy` out loud, so writing "owner" there is visible, while writing "owner" into `ratifiedBy` was silent AND switched off the check on `allowedBy` at the same time. So a non-null `ratifiedBy` has to carry a day, as YYYY-MM-DD, and a place a reader can go and look -- a commit id, a path, a file, a URL. Only the SHAPE is checked. Nothing here can tell whether the place says what the line claims, and nothing here pretends to; resolving the citation with `git cat-file -e` was weighed and dropped, because it costs the suite its ability to run on a tree without that history and forces every ratification to be a commit. Both halves are now printed by the gate.

HOW LONG AN UNRATIFIED LINE MAY LIVE. `expires` was the only pressure, and it presses on the LINE rather than on the owner -- while the date is moved by the same party that never asked, for free, as often as it likes. Nothing counted that, so `ratifiedBy: null` could survive for ever in fortnight steps, each step an ordinary-looking diff. `renewals` counts the moves, and the rule is one: unratified, a line may be extended ONCE; a second extension needs a name in `ratifiedBy`, or the point fixed and the line deleted. WHAT IT COSTS: the counter is written by hand and can be written down. What it buys is that an uncounted renewal is then a deliberate lie sitting in a diff, where the defect it replaces was forgetfulness.

NONE OF THIS IS A BOUNDARY, and a reader who does not know that will think the machinery is stronger than it is. Whoever can edit this file can edit `tests/stand/allowance.ts` in the same commit; every rule above is one deletion away from gone. These checks buy exactly one thing -- that the false sentence has to be written ON PURPOSE, and lands in a diff where somebody can see it. They cost nothing against a determined author and they were never meant to. The defect they were built for was carelessness: five lines saying the owner had agreed, written in one sitting because it was the easiest thing to type.

Why it exists. `pnpm run test:stand` exits 1 on this revision, and not because the stand is broken: points 6 and 7 are red about the product in every run measured, and they belong to a step that has not happened -- Ш7, the restore traps. Point 1 is the third line and it is not that: it comes and goes with the window the stand is handed, which is the paragraph below. A gate that took the stand as it is would be red until Ш7 lands, and a `pre-push` hook over a permanently red gate is a hook that comes off with the first `--no-verify`.

HOW MANY POINTS ARE RED depends on the run, and 2026-08-25 (Ш8) found out WHY. It depends on one thing: whether Cursor restores a "New Agent" editor into the window. That editor lives in an editor part of its own, the grid does not hold it, and `vscode.window.tabGroups.all` lists it all the same -- which is the line the stand has been printing all along, "the grid accounted for 2, 2, 1, 1 of them, which is the editor holding a tab group outside its own grid". Over the ten runs measured BEFORE that day's repairs its presence predicted the colour of points 1, 3 and 4 every time; after them it was REPORTED to predict point 1 and nothing else, and that report is false -- see "WHAT THE FIFTH RUN SETTLED" below. It predicts all three, before those repairs and after them. It is not the queue, and it is not arithmetic anybody got wrong -- the observer writes down exactly what the two APIs answer. So the redness is admitted here rather than ignored there, and the admission is held to five things a comment could not hold it to. A point that goes red without a line here is red. A point red by MORE than its `atMost` is red. A point that comes back GREEN is red -- take the line out -- unless its line carries `mayBeGreen: true`, which needs the runs behind it written into `seen`. Every line stops working on `expires`, whatever else is true. And `cap` is how many lines may live at once: a new one is written after an old one is taken out, not beside it. Three of the five are in use as this is written, and the two that came free on 2026-08-25 are what a ceiling with room under it is for.

`expires`, `cap`, `renewals` and the `allowedBy` / `ratifiedBy` pair are asserted by `tests/stand/allowance.test.ts`, which needs no editor and runs on every `npx jest`. That is the difference between a deadline and a note about one, and between a signature and a name somebody typed.

WHY A CEILING AND NOT AN EXACT NUMBER. The design this was built to was stricter: a point red by LESS than its line said was to be refused too, so that a budget nobody tightens could not quietly become a permission with no end. That rule presumes the stand's answer is a function of the product. It is not, and 2026-08-25 is the measurement -- runs of the stand on one revision with nothing changed between them:

`.` is green. SIX IS A FLOOR, NOT A COUNT, and that is said here because this file first said five while a report of the same step said six. `tests/stand/run.mjs` deletes `.vscode-test/stand-output/` at the start of every run (`prepare()`), so a run's numbers survive exactly until the next run starts: rows 1 to 5 are transcribed from runs whose recordings no longer exist and cannot be re-read by anybody, here or later. Row 6 could be re-read when this was written and cannot be now: the runs of that day overwrote it, and what stands at `.vscode-test/stand-output/verdict.json` today is the gate run of 2026-08-25T06:39:43Z -- a different run with different numbers, 0 to 5 and 8 green and 6 and 7 at three. `.gate/receipts.ndjson` records eight gate-driven stand runs as this is written, up from the four it had then; a standalone `pnpm run test:stand` leaves no receipt at all, so the total is not established and no number here should be read as one.

Point 1 -- the accumulating editor groups, the defect the stand was built for -- came back green in two runs of six. Point 3 moved 1, 2, 2, 2, 3, 1 and point 7 moved 3, 3, 3, 3, 2, 3, so BOTH directions of the exact rule fire on noise: run 5 would have been refused for being better at point 7, and runs 1 and 6 for being better at points 1 and 3. An exact number over a random variable is a coin, and a gate that is a coin teaches a person to run it again instead of reading it, which is the one thing the plan says a gate must never do. The plan's own Ш9 anticipates exactly this shape: 'if the miss is really one in ten, a green run is unreachable, and the rule has to be `the miss rate did not grow`'.

The exact rule is therefore kept where it is sound and named where it is not: a line whose `atMost` equals what the point always returns IS the exact rule, and `mayBeGreen` is the escape, per line, with its evidence beside it. The pressure to shrink rests on `expires` and `cap`, which are machine-enforced and need no reproducibility at all.

How to take a line out: fix the point, run `pnpm run gate`, delete the line. The gate refuses a line whose point is green unless the line admits green, so a fixed defect cannot leave its permission behind. A line that DOES admit green is outside that check by construction: points 3 and 4 were, and they went out on 2026-08-25 because four runs said so and a person read them, which is the part nothing here does for anybody.

`atMost` is `Finding.violations` from `tests/stand/judge.ts` -- how many named things went wrong at that point, as an integer. It is not a physical magnitude and two points' numbers do not compare with each other; the magnitude a person needs is in `measured`, which nothing checks.

Read by the gate to decide a colour: `point`, `answer`, `atMost`, `mayBeGreen`, `expires`, `cap`, `renewals`. Read by the gate and printed on every full run: `allowedBy`, `ratifiedBy`, `renewals`. Read by people: `says`, `seen`, `measured`, `why`.

THE OTHER KIND OF LINE, added by Ш9 on 2026-08-25: `rates`. An admitted POINT is a named thing the stand found wrong; a RATE is how many of N attempts at one editor command missed. Ш9's own words anticipated it -- "if the miss is really one in ten, a green run is unreachable, and the rule has to be `the miss rate did not grow`" -- and the measurement that day said the opposite of what the plan feared, so the ceiling below is NOUGHT and the rule is green. The machinery is here anyway, because the thing being measured is a FORK's workbench and it ships every few days: the day the miss comes back, the decision is one number and one date in this file, in front of a reader, rather than an edit to a test.

WHAT A RATE LINE CARRIES THAT A POINT'S DOES NOT: `of`, the number of attempts the ceiling was measured over. A rate is a fraction and this file stores only its numerator, so nought misses out of one and nought out of ten would otherwise be the same sentence -- and the first is what a probe that quietly gave up looks like. A run of fewer attempts than `of` is refused rather than compared.

WHAT IS DIFFERENT ABOUT A CEILING OF NOUGHT. It admits nothing, so it is not a permission, so the ONE-RENEWAL rule does not apply to it: `expires` still fires and forces somebody to measure again, and `renewals` may climb as often as the fork ships. Asking the owner to sign every eight weeks for a check that has never been red would teach signing as a way to make a colour go away. The moment `atMost` goes above nought the line becomes a permission and the one-renewal rule applies to it exactly as it does to a point.

WHAT THE CURSOR STAGE CANNOT COVER, AND IT IS NOT A CHOICE. Measured 2026-08-25 over three launches and two launchers, polling thirty seconds each: Cursor's extension TEST host -- any window carrying `--extensionTestsPath` -- registers no third-party extension at all, neither developed nor installed. `vscode.extensions.all` answers 48 entries, every one of them Cursor's own, where the same arguments against VS Code 1.134.0 answer 100 including ours. So the live suites cannot run in Cursor: every one of them opens by asserting the extension is there. And the same host exits 0 on a failing run, where VS Code exits 1 on the same file -- which is why this budget is read against a file the probe WRITES and never against an exit code. The product in Cursor is covered by `pnpm run test:stand`, which uses a DEV host, where the extension does load.
